blocks.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.

people.name: Elspeth Moravec
people.role: transport researcher who surveyed night-train passengers

people.name: Gideon Sarkis
people.role: former timetable planner for a large rail operator

people.name: Corinna Valtonen
people.role: teacher who regularly travels by night train

paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, falling asleep in one city and waking up in another was an ordinary part of European travel. Sleeper carriages linked capitals across the continent, and for many families an overnight journey was the only affordable way to reach a distant coast or visit relatives abroad. By the early 2000s, however, that world seemed to be fading. Low-cost airlines could carry passengers across the continent in a couple of hours for less than the price of a bunk, while new high-speed lines made many daytime rail journeys short enough to finish before dinner. One by one, overnight routes were cut from the timetables.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The trouble was partly financial. Night services are expensive to operate: a sleeping car holds far fewer people than an ordinary carriage, and because the train spends the night on a single long journey, it cannot be used for several shorter trips during the day, as a normal train would be. In 2016 Germany's national rail operator withdrew its own sleeper services, arguing that they had been losing money for years. Many observers assumed that this decision marked the end of the story.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: It did not. Austria's state railway took over several of the abandoned routes and began investing in new carriages, betting that demand had been underestimated rather than lost. Within a few years the gamble appeared to be paying off, and other operators followed its example. Today, travellers can once again board an evening train in cities such as Vienna, Zurich or Brussels and step off the next morning hundreds of kilometres away. On some lines, demand has been so strong that tickets for summer weekends sell out months in advance. A handful of new routes have also been launched by small private companies, some of which hire their locomotives and carriages instead of buying them, a way of keeping start-up costs low.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Part of the explanation lies in changing attitudes to flying. A growing number of travellers, particularly younger ones, say they want to reduce the carbon footprint of their holidays, and rail produces far lower emissions per passenger than air travel over the same distance. Yet according to transport researcher Elspeth Moravec, concern for the planet is only part of the picture. In a survey of more than two thousand passengers on four overnight routes, she found that the reason given most often for choosing the train was a practical one: it saved the cost of a hotel room. "People like to feel virtuous," she says, "but what really persuades them is arriving in the city centre, rested, without having paid for an extra night's accommodation." Environmental motives came second, ahead of comfort and a dislike of airport security queues.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Not everyone is convinced the revival will last. Gideon Sarkis, who spent twenty years planning timetables for a large operator, points out that night trains face obstacles that daytime services rarely meet. Track maintenance is usually carried out after dark, so overnight trains are sometimes sent on slower diversions, and each country along the route may charge its own fee for using the rails. "A train crossing three borders can receive three separate bills," he explains, "and in the end it is the passengers who cover the difference." In his view, ticket prices will remain the biggest barrier unless governments agree on common rules for charging trains that cross their borders. He is not against night trains, he stresses; he simply wants their supporters to be realistic.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Passengers themselves report mixed experiences. Fares vary enormously, from the price of a reclining seat to several hundred euros for a private compartment with its own shower. Delays are common, and some newer carriages have been criticised for being cramped. Food on board is usually simple, often little more than a bread roll and coffee at breakfast. Even so, many travellers describe the journey as an experience in itself. Corinna Valtonen, a teacher who regularly takes an overnight service to visit her sister in another country, compares it to "a small hotel that happens to move". She admits that she rarely sleeps through the night, but says the hours spent reading or watching the countryside slip past the window are part of the pleasure rather than time wasted.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Whether night trains become a mainstream choice again may depend less on nostalgia than on investment. Operators need new rolling stock, which can take years to design and build, and booking a journey that crosses several national networks is still far more complicated than buying a plane ticket. Moravec believes that a single booking website covering every European operator would do more for night trains than any advertising campaign. For now, though, the sight of a sleeper pulling out of a station at dusk is no longer a scene from a museum. It is, once again, simply a way of getting somewhere.
paragraphs.label: G

section.text:
All Aboard the Night Train

A. For much of the twentieth century, falling asleep in one city and waking up in another was an ordinary part of European travel. Sleeper carriages linked capitals across the continent, and for many families an overnight journey was the only affordable way to reach a distant coast or visit relatives abroad. By the early 2000s, however, that world seemed to be fading. Low-cost airlines could carry passengers across the continent in a couple of hours for less than the price of a bunk, while new high-speed lines made many daytime rail journeys short enough to finish before dinner. One by one, overnight routes were cut from the timetables.

B. The trouble was partly financial. Night services are expensive to operate: a sleeping car holds far fewer people than an ordinary carriage, and because the train spends the night on a single long journey, it cannot be used for several shorter trips during the day, as a normal train would be. In 2016 Germany's national rail operator withdrew its own sleeper services, arguing that they had been losing money for years. Many observers assumed that this decision marked the end of the story.

C. It did not. Austria's state railway took over several of the abandoned routes and began investing in new carriages, betting that demand had been underestimated rather than lost. Within a few years the gamble appeared to be paying off, and other operators followed its example. Today, travellers can once again board an evening train in cities such as Vienna, Zurich or Brussels and step off the next morning hundreds of kilometres away. On some lines, demand has been so strong that tickets for summer weekends sell out months in advance. A handful of new routes have also been launched by small private companies, some of which hire their locomotives and carriages instead of buying them, a way of keeping start-up costs low.

D. Part of the explanation lies in changing attitudes to flying. A growing number of travellers, particularly younger ones, say they want to reduce the carbon footprint of their holidays, and rail produces far lower emissions per passenger than air travel over the same distance. Yet according to transport researcher Elspeth Moravec, concern for the planet is only part of the picture. In a survey of more than two thousand passengers on four overnight routes, she found that the reason given most often for choosing the train was a practical one: it saved the cost of a hotel room. "People like to feel virtuous," she says, "but what really persuades them is arriving in the city centre, rested, without having paid for an extra night's accommodation." Environmental motives came second, ahead of comfort and a dislike of airport security queues.

E. Not everyone is convinced the revival will last. Gideon Sarkis, who spent twenty years planning timetables for a large operator, points out that night trains face obstacles that daytime services rarely meet. Track maintenance is usually carried out after dark, so overnight trains are sometimes sent on slower diversions, and each country along the route may charge its own fee for using the rails. "A train crossing three borders can receive three separate bills," he explains, "and in the end it is the passengers who cover the difference." In his view, ticket prices will remain the biggest barrier unless governments agree on common rules for charging trains that cross their borders. He is not against night trains, he stresses; he simply wants their supporters to be realistic.

F. Passengers themselves report mixed experiences. Fares vary enormously, from the price of a reclining seat to several hundred euros for a private compartment with its own shower. Delays are common, and some newer carriages have been criticised for being cramped. Food on board is usually simple, often little more than a bread roll and coffee at breakfast. Even so, many travellers describe the journey as an experience in itself. Corinna Valtonen, a teacher who regularly takes an overnight service to visit her sister in another country, compares it to "a small hotel that happens to move". She admits that she rarely sleeps through the night, but says the hours spent reading or watching the countryside slip past the window are part of the pleasure rather than time wasted.

G. Whether night trains become a mainstream choice again may depend less on nostalgia than on investment. Operators need new rolling stock, which can take years to design and build, and booking a journey that crosses several national networks is still far more complicated than buying a plane ticket. Moravec believes that a single booking website covering every European operator would do more for night trains than any advertising campaign. For now, though, the sight of a sleeper pulling out of a station at dusk is no longer a scene from a museum. It is, once again, simply a way of getting somewhere.
